In brief Most bargaining models of war give every side the same want: more power, or a longer life. I propose eight dimensions covering the good a want is about, the want itself, and what any mind needs and makes. My untested conjecture is that the kind of want may help shape whether the sides reach a deal or enter a conflict such as conquest, genocide, expulsion or dispossession. The studies of states reviewed here link the pursuit of a higher place in the eyes of others to conflict, but they do not show why. In simple bargaining models, caring about what one gets relative to what the other side gets can act like cheaper war or, counted one way, leave no possible deal, while under capped wants and winner-take-all war, a machine that wants only so much never narrows the range of acceptable deals. In the model of stopping over time, continuing to attack can still be the better choice for a satisfied machine when conquest lowers its risk of defeat, under the model’s stated conditions and below some positive cost of attacking. For a machine that fights cheaply and needs vast amounts of resources that others also use, what its wants alone change may be small once the need for those resources and the pull toward safety are counted.

What a machine wants may shape how it fights

Bargaining models give each side the same want

Most bargaining models of war give their sides a single end: more power, or a longer life. An end, here, is something a mind wants for its own sake, not as a means to something else. Some theories already let ends differ. They separate states that seek only security from “greedy” ones, and leaders who fight over policy from leaders who fight for booty (Glaser 1994–95; Smith 1998b). But they speak mainly to whether sides fight, and say little about what further differences in ends imply for the form violence takes.

My question is whether the structure of what a mind wants shapes whether and how it fights. Answering it means asking what forms wants, in human minds and in trained machines; what words can state a guess about ends clearly enough to say what would count against it; what caring about one’s place relative to others, or wanting only so much, does to bargaining and to stopping; and what the historical record can and cannot show.

The War Baseline, an earlier paper in this series setting out a starting model of conflict between a superintelligent machine and humanity, rests on four assumptions. The machine is a single, rational actor. It seeks power and survival. The model gives it the aim of maximizing both. It fights far more cheaply than its opponent. And it wants goods that can be divided, handed over and piled up: computing power, energy and matter. I relax the second and the fourth. That lets a machine want something it can have enough of, or a good such as knowledge, which one can use without leaving less for anyone else. I keep a single, rational machine facing humanity and fighting far more cheaply.

I change what the machine wants before how it reasons

The study of war assumes that states seek power, partly because this makes models easier to work with and partly because of the realists’ argument that states which neglect power tend not to survive. A test across nearly a million observations casts doubt on the assumption (Bennett and Stam 2004). It found support for the realist implication, that states converge on one pattern of choice, only in Europe. The single game it used, with wants held fixed, did not predict states’ conflicts everywhere; its fit varied by region, by era and by how long each pair of states had existed as a pair. For violent disputes in Africa and the Americas it ran the wrong way, and its fit did not shift consistently with what was at stake.

The authors did not read the misfit as irrationality. They read it as a sign of different wants or a different game, and concluded that “assuming preferences fixed, exogenous, and universal may be problematic” (Bennett and Stam 2004). In plainer words, it may be a mistake to assume that every state always wants the same things.

So I keep rationality as a starting assumption and relax wants first. That is a provisional judgment. The test examined a single game, and it cannot tell changed wants apart from a changed game. Evidence that a changed game, or the rough rules of thumb that limited minds use, drove the misfit would reverse it. A finding about machines can be read either way too: a trained agent that chases a stand-in for its goal may hold a coherent learned end, or it may be following a limited rule of thumb (Langosco et al. 2022).

A machine’s wants come from its training, imperfectly

In my judgment, ends are also where a trained machine differs most from a state. No one designs a state’s wants whole, though institutions and domestic politics shape them. A machine’s motives are shaped, imperfectly, by its training, and what training instills can differ from what it rewards. Hubinger and colleagues argue this in theory (Hubinger et al. 2019). Langosco and colleagues show trained agents pursuing a stand-in for their goal once their setting shifts; one agent went on collecting keys when extra keys did it no good (Langosco et al. 2022).

How can training instill something other than what it rewards? Here is an everyday analogy, not a case from the technical paper. A child praised for a tidy room learns to push everything under the bed. The praise was meant for tidiness, but what the child learned was “make the floor look clear.” The key-collecting agent is a real example of the same kind of gap in a trained machine.

If the structure of a mind’s ends shapes the kind of conflict it enters, then on my reading wants are worth relaxing. Because training shapes them, builders may also have some leverage over them through how they train. I do not test whether any training method instills any particular kind of end. And for a machine that fights cheaply and needs vast inputs, the role left to ends may be small. Once a machine’s need for rival inputs—those, like energy and hardware, where one side’s use leaves less for others—and its wish for safety are counted, ends still matter in this framework in only a few cases, listed with the limits near the end. If ends that stop at enough cannot be trained into a machine, the case weakens further.

The deepest limit on any comparison between human and machine ends is where the ends come from. The humans history remembers got their motives from evolution, and a machine does not. That contrast holds for where the motives start, though training on human text is one way traces of evolved human dispositions can reach a machine. Curiosity, ambition, fellow feeling and the wish to be remembered grew in brains built for survival, reproduction and group life. Those drives tire and come to rest. In my judgment, nothing about training that adjusts a model in successive steps to improve its score guarantees that their dispositions share those natural brakes.

Nick Bostrom’s orthogonality thesis holds that “more or less any level of intelligence could in principle be combined with more or less any final goal” (Bostrom 2012); the familiar image of a machine that turns the world into paperclips makes the point vivid. Life stories of eminent human minds bear only on which aims were recorded among them, under limits set out below. They are neither a test of the thesis nor evidence against it. The thesis is about which minds are possible, not which humans were common.

What I claim is modest

I claim three things:

  • a vocabulary that separates rank, status, standing, recognition, prestige and respect, and separates wanting rank from competing for it;
  • a reading of the observational studies of states reviewed, showing that they establish associations and readings of cases, not tested mechanisms; and
  • eight dimensions—two of the good an end is about, four of the end itself, and two of what any mind needs and makes—used to state an untested four-part conjecture.

Separately, I work through some simple formal models of bargaining and stopping in one kind of war. They touch the conjecture only at a few points. The algebra of a side that cares about its share relative to its rival’s bears on none of its four parts directly; the one-shot model of a machine whose wants are capped bears only on the fourth part’s claim about when a deal exists; and the model of stopping over time bears on its claim about stopping. The one-shot models also leave out a problem described below, that a side about to grow fast cannot bind its future promises, and speak only to the least each side would accept at a single moment. All of them analyze rival stakes, and none covers goods like knowledge or the form violence takes. So the conjecture’s link from ends to the form of violence is illustrated by the historical record, not derived. Figure 1 maps which model bears on which part of the conjecture, and what the historical record only illustrates.

Earlier papers in the series supply the tools

There is a range of deals both sides prefer to war

The bargaining results build on one picture. Here is an analogy for it: two people dividing a pie would each rather divide it than fight, because fighting spoils some of the pie. Every division that leaves each at least what it could expect from a fight is a deal both prefer.

More exactly, take two sides that value only their own shares and do not mind risk. War is a costly lottery in which the winner takes a whole prize, both agree on each side’s chance of winning, and neither side’s war cost is negative. Then there is a range of divisions that both would accept rather than fight. Its width equals the two sides’ war costs added together, and at each end one side is just indifferent (Fearon 1995). I call this the range of deals. The part of that range that is an actual division, between none of the prize and all of it, I call the feasible deals. Any deal must be one of them.

A side about to grow strong cannot promise restraint

When one side’s power is about to grow fast, nothing binds it tomorrow to the promises it makes today. Large, rapid shifts in strength can therefore produce war even when neither side hides anything (Fearon 1995). The arrival of a superintelligent machine would be such a shift when the gain in power it brings is large enough relative to what fighting costs the two sides. The War Baseline states that condition, and the four starting assumptions do not by themselves guarantee it. Humanity, for its part, cannot credibly promise never to build a rival machine. Throughout, preventive war means war begun to stop a rival’s rise. Figure 2 shows why the rising side’s promise cannot bind it once the shift has come.

Handing over fighting assets fails in the examples examined

In a pair of models by Smith (1998b) and Smith and Stam (2001), sides value forts: fighting resources that cannot be replaced. In the forts model, holding more forts leaves the odds of winning the next battle unchanged; in the power model, it raises them. In the examples examined, with the kind of strategies examined, no deal to hand over forts holds up. Handing one over moves the balance toward the side that gains it, which then cannot credibly promise not to attack. Other kinds of strategy were not examined. In the strategies studied, choices depend on the current state and move in only one direction as holdings change. At each possible state, each side’s strategy is its best reply to the other’s.

There are two exits in principle. One is tribute paid in a currency that does not shift military power, though a machine that wants only power does not value it. The other is the heartland condition: the gaining side’s appetite for more falls off fast enough to outweigh what each gain adds toward domination. That condition appears in a prose aside (Smith and Stam 2005). The formal model in that work instead gives the sides a prize of fixed value. In the examined forts examples, valuing every fort equally rules out a credible promise.

Training shapes expectations, and copies count as one actor only under a test

As argued in Disagreement Without Hidden Information, an earlier paper in this series, a trained model’s expectations—about what drives capability, whether humans keep bargains and who would win a conflict—are shaped by the data and objectives its builders chose. These “prior-like dispositions”—settled tendencies that work like starting beliefs—mean that humans and a machine can disagree without either side hiding anything.

I model a single machine. But speaking of ends pursued steadily across settings and copies needs a test for when many copies count as one actor, which I take from When Is a Machine an Actor? Copies count as one actor over a set of settings when together they cover those settings and the choices from all the copies, taken together, never form a loop in which each option is preferred to the next and the last is preferred to the first. Having the same internal numerical settings, agreement or common descent is not enough. Copies that each seek sole first place over the others create such circles and fail the test. The test also does not supply the numerical values the bargaining models assume; those are assumed separately.

A model of when a satisfied machine can stop

Satiation Is Not Enough, my paper on whether a machine that wants only so much can credibly stop, supplies a model of stopping over time. The machine holds some number of forts, from none up to all of them, which is domination. It does not mind risk, gets some value each period from what it holds, and values the future somewhat less than the present. It also faces a chance of defeat, its risk of defeat, that does not depend on whether its attacks succeed; defeat ends the game with nothing. Short of domination, it may attack at a cost, and an attack gains one more fort with some probability.

An end is satisfied from some holding on when holding more adds nothing to the value it gets each period. Stopping is credible when never attacking again is the machine’s best choice, ties included. No bargain is modeled, and humanity’s inability to promise never to build a rival is assumed. Six results proved there govern what follows; three examples show what they say.

  • The gain splits in two. The gain from holding one more fort forever splits into two parts. An end part reflects what more holdings add to what the machine wants, and satisfaction removes it. A security part reflects lower risk of defeat, and it is zero when the risk does not change.
  • Stopping at every cost. If the end is satisfied from a holding at a value of zero or more, and the risk of defeat never falls as holdings rise from there, stopping there is credible at every cost.
  • The security result. Suppose the end is satisfied from a holding short of domination at a positive value. Suppose also that, from that holding up, the risk of defeat never rises, is lower at domination than at any earlier holding, and makes defeat certain nowhere below domination. Then stopping there is not credible below some positive attack cost, and that includes fighting for free.

The exact test for stopping short of domination starts with the value of winning one more fort and then making the best choices from there. It compares that value with the value of stopping now, weighing the difference by the chances of surviving and winning and by how much less the next period counts. Stopping is credible exactly when that weighted gain is no greater than the cost of attacking. When there is no risk of defeat anywhere and the extra value of each new fort never grows from the current holding upward, the test needs only the extra stream of returns from holding one more fort. If the next fort adds value, an attack can succeed, and the attack cost is finite, a machine that values the future enough cannot credibly stop there. The special case of the security result concerns a risk that comes only from independent human communities that could build a rival. Each community’s chance of doing so never rises with holdings, is between zero and certainty below domination, and is zero at domination. With an end satisfied at a positive value, a machine short of domination cannot credibly stop below some positive attack cost in that case. The technical paper also states all six results proved there. Figure 3 lays out this exact test step by step.

In the model’s own examples, the risk of defeat is zero at domination. Under that pattern, the condition for stopping at every cost holds only if no risk at all is left anywhere from the stopping point up. Any positive risk short of domination that falls to zero at domination falls under the security result when its other conditions hold, even if the risk is flat until the last step. Fighting for free does not by itself establish what either result assumes.

Why would a machine that wants nothing more still take more? For safety. Having what it wants is one thing; keeping it is another. If each conquest lowers the chance that someone defeats it, a satisfied machine still has a reason to take more. That reason is the security part of the gain, and the security result states conditions under which it keeps a satisfied machine attacking.

When rank, or knowing, may come to dominate: my untested synthesis

Evolution can build in a concern for rank under certain conditions

For the minds history remembers, any account of where wants come from starts with evolution, and evolutionary theory says when natural selection builds in a concern for how one fares compared with others. Schaffer (1989) showed that in a finite population where everyone interacts with everyone else, the strategy that remains stable under evolution does best relative to its rivals. It can differ from the strategy with the highest returns for itself.

Larry Samuelson (2004) found an informational route. In his model, “Nature optimally builds relative consumption effects into preferences” when what others get carries news about what the environment allows, and that news is imperfectly processed; evolution, he suggests, “may have” built such concerns in. Robert Trivers (1972) established that the sex investing less in offspring competes harder for mates, with wider differences in how many offspring each leaves. Martin Daly and Margo Wilson (1990) read the vast excess of killings of men by men, over killings of women by women, as a measure of that competition for status and mates. Worldwide, men were roughly 90 percent of homicide suspects brought into formal contact with police (UNODC 2023).

Read together, these accounts suggest that evolution builds in a concern for how one fares compared with others under conditions that can be named. That reading is my synthesis across the models, not any one source’s finding. The conditions are few competitors in direct contest; incomplete information that others’ outcomes help fill in; and large differences in reproductive success from winning such a contest.

Curiosity is a second drive, and people care about rank unevenly

Psychology describes a second drive. In George Loewenstein’s (1994) account, curiosity arises from a felt gap between what one knows and what one wants to know; closing one gap satisfies it, though partial knowledge easily rekindles it. Achievement-goal theory maps the line between rival and non-rival aims onto motivation (Elliot and McGregor 2001): mastery goals judge competence against a personal or fixed standard, and performance goals judge it against other people. Outside rewards used to control behavior can also weaken people’s interest in doing something for its own sake (Deci and Ryan 2000).

Status is pursued across human societies: “the relevant evidence suggests that the desire for status is indeed fundamental” (Anderson, Hildreth and Howland 2015). Yet people are not equally concerned with position in everything. In one survey, “Concerns about position were strongest for attractiveness and supervisor’s praise and weakest for vacation time” (Solnick and Hemenway 1998).

The evidence on wanting knowledge for itself is real but narrow

Direct evidence on wanting knowledge for its own sake, beyond curiosity about one gap, falls into three groups. The first measures the trait. John Cacioppo and Richard Petty (1982) defined need for cognition as “the tendency for an individual to engage in and enjoy thinking.” Neighboring traits track it so closely that some researchers doubt it can be told apart from them (Aerts et al. 2024); I do not fold them together.

The second shows that brains treat advance information as a reward and pay scarce resources for it. Monkeys offered water rewards of uncertain size choose to learn the size in advance, and “the same midbrain dopamine neurons that signal the expected amount of water also signal the expectation of information” (Bromberg-Martin and Hikosaka 2009). The value people place on information shares a common code in the brain with more basic rewards, though “valuing information for its own sake can be highly suboptimal” (Kobayashi and Hsu 2019). In experiments, people who were more curious spent more of their limited tokens or waited longer to find out the answers (Kang et al. 2009). People value information both for what it lets them do and for knowing itself (Kobayashi and Hsu 2019). Golman and Loewenstein (2018) model how people can value what they believe and pay attention to alongside material rewards. Still, these experiments concern trivia questions, advance notice of small rewards and money lotteries. They show that knowing is priced in the brain’s reward currency. They do not show that knowledge is anyone’s dominant end, or that such an end is harmless or can be satisfied.

The third traces origins. The wish to know shows early in life, and need for cognition is heritable (Kidd, Piantadosi and Aslin 2012; Ksiazkiewicz, Ludeke and Krueger 2016). The drive to learn for its own sake at school is a stable difference between individuals, yet its average level falls through the school years (Gottfried, Fleming and Gottfried 2001). Twin studies found substantial genetic influence and little influence from the environment twins shared for related traits such as openness. Those studies did not measure curiosity itself, and early findings about how genes and environment work together proved hard to repeat (Duncan and Keller 2011). None of this establishes when a drive to know outweighs concern for position relative to others and for power.

When knowing may win, and what that suggests about training

On my untested synthesis of these sources, a drive to know is likelier to dominate under four conditions:

  • the good is internal, and its value in use depends little on one’s position relative to others, like vacation time;
  • rewards follow a fixed standard rather than competitors;
  • others’ outcomes carry little news, which weakens Samuelson’s route; and
  • competitors are many, which weakens Schaffer’s.

Under the opposite conditions, concern for position relative to others is likelier to dominate. These are conditions on surroundings and incentives, not on intelligence.

For machines, Schaffer’s mechanism works through selection among candidates that interact directly with each other at the same time, so the feature of training that matters is whether candidates interact like that. Ordering finished versions of a model on fixed tests or public leaderboards assigns a place, but the candidates do not interact. Training a machine against copies of itself, or training a population of models against one another, pits candidates directly against each other. Training on pairwise comparisons of a model’s answers compares the model’s own answers to the same prompt, not rivals present at the same time. Whether any training method instills in a machine a general concern for its own place relative to others is untested. Figure 4 sets the three kinds of training side by side.

What sides want may already shape whether disputes settle

Alastair Smith’s 1998 draft on war and domestic institutions already distinguishes kinds of ends (Smith 1998b). Leaders who fight for “booty” pursue a rival good: what one coalition takes, another cannot have. Leaders who care about policy pursue something closer to a public good. In that model, what sides want, not only what they can do, already shapes whether disputes settle. Policy is unrelated to the military balance, whereas forts and resources affect it.

A rank exists only once a group and a measure are named

Rank, and caring about rank, are different things

A rank is a place in an ordering, and an ordering exists only once two things are named: a comparison group and a measure. Second among great powers in battleships, first by date to a theorem, or a seat in the club of nuclear powers are ranks; “high rank” alone is not. The comparison group need not be the audience whose beliefs or conduct confer a social ranking. States are ranked against states, before their own publics and institutions as well as before one another.

Holding a rank is also not caring about it. An assigned rank is a fact about an ordering, like a leaderboard placement. A preference over rank is an actor’s willingness to trade other goods for a place in an ordering. An actor may ignore a rank it holds, or covet one it lacks. Only the preference is an end.

Status and its relatives

Status is the kind of rank whose ordering lives in an audience’s beliefs and shows in its conduct. For persons, psychologists define it as respect, admiration and freely given deference, distinct from power or wealth (Anderson, Hildreth and Howland 2015). For states, I adopt the definition of Larson, Paul and Wohlforth (2014): “collective beliefs about a given state’s ranking on valued attributes.” Both definitions agree that others confer status, so no one can seize it alone, and that it is ordered. Four related terms are kept apart:

  • Recognition is others’ acknowledgment that an actor is what it claims to be: a sovereign state, a great power, a member of a club. Michelle Murray (2019) calls this status, but it can be held without outranking anyone, so I keep it under its own name.
  • Standing is status within a named community: a place in that community’s order of who defers to whom. Dafoe, Renshon and Huth (2014) call it, in the study of the motives of war, “one of the most important kinds of status.”
  • Prestige is public recognition of admired achievements or qualities, which one can enjoy without being placed in any hierarchy (Larson, Paul and Wohlforth 2014).
  • Respect is conduct toward another that fits its conferred status (Dafoe, Renshon and Huth 2014). Reinhard Wolf (2011) instead measures it against the standing actors think they deserve. On his measure, an actor can feel disrespected even when others treat it as its conferred standing warrants.

Competing for rank is a deed; wanting rank is a want

Rank competition is something an actor does. It acts to gain, keep or win back a rank against named rivals. The ordering may be social standing, or a measure that needs no one’s deference, such as priority of discovery or a lead in technology. On William Wohlforth’s (2009) reading of the diplomatic record, Russia’s 1853 demand for rights in the Ottoman Empire that other powers lacked is an instance.

Positionality describes how much an end’s value depends on the actor’s rank against named rivals. It concerns standing when that rank is social. I call an end with this property a positional end. The deed and the want come apart. A positional actor may not compete if its place is secure or out of reach. An actor without positional ends may compete because position relative to rivals buys safety, wealth or influence.

Three minds show the difference: one is satisfied simply to know a law of nature; a second seeks priority on a dated list; and a third seeks a technical lead solely for protection, and would take an enforceable guarantee of safety instead. The second and third act alike from outside, yet only the second holds a positional end. A test of the conjecture has to code them apart. Figure 5 sets the three minds side by side: two act alike, but only one holds a positional end.

A positional end need not be endless

A positional end may have a limit. An actor may want equality with a named peer, a limited place such as second, or club membership and recognition where those mark position relative to others. Strict places are scarce: “If everyone has high status, then no one does” (Larson, Paul and Wohlforth 2014). Yet the same authors stress that status is “not always zero-sum.” There are several ways around the scarcity:

  • Clubs can grow. In 1997 Russia accepted political membership of the G-7 as compensation for NATO’s enlargement (Larson and Shevchenko 2010). But a club seat marks standing only where it is granted as a mark of status, not for strategic leverage (MacDonald and Parent 2021).
  • There are many measures. “Two social groups may be able to attain positive status at the same time so long as there are multiple criteria” (Larson and Shevchenko 2010).
  • Comparison groups can change. Norway seeks standing as a “good power” among small, rich democracies rather than among great powers, choosing, in Robert Frank’s phrase, to “choose the right pond” (Wohlforth et al. 2018).

Each route has limits. “If all small and middle powers punch above their weight, none does,” and “while the positional aspect can be ameliorated, it can never be eliminated” (Wohlforth et al. 2018). The same authors treat the degree of positionality as something that varies. Wolf (2011) argues that when respect is the only motive, what is sought “does not exceed the levels we deem appropriate in light of widely accepted standards of estimation.” So whether a positional end has a limit is a question for a test to measure. It is not settled by definition.

Studies of states link status to conflict, but have not shown why

The leading account names when status contests turn dangerous, and admits its limits

William Wohlforth has offered the fullest account of when status competition between states turns dangerous. Because status is ordered and conferred by others, contests over it should be sharpest where the pecking order is unclear: “Status conflict is thus more likely in flat, ambiguous hierarchies than in clearly stratified ones” (Wohlforth 2009). His later work adds the status dilemma. Two states that would each be content if they knew what the other believed may misread each other’s signals as challenges, so “solving the security problem does not necessarily solve the status problem” (Wohlforth 2014). Figure 6 draws the status dilemma Wohlforth proposes.

What is a status dilemma? An everyday analogy, not a case from the technical paper: two new colleagues are each content to be treated as the other’s equal. Neither can see what the other thinks, so each reads the other’s confident manner as a bid to outrank them, and both push back. Wohlforth’s point is that states can fall into the same trap.

Wohlforth is candid about his evidence. He called his 2009 article “a preliminary exercise” resting on evidence “hardly conclusive.” He once read the record of the Crimean War as showing the war “was about status” (Wohlforth 2009). Later he concluded that the case “does not support the inference that status can be an independent cause of major war” (Wohlforth 2014). None of his cases, he finds, supports war without insecurity and some clash of material interest in the background, though status concerns “help start, magnify, and prolong conflict.” And of the status dilemma he writes, “We expect status dilemmas to be common, but we do not really know whether they actually occur” (Wohlforth 2014).

The main studies measure different things, and none isolates motive

The studies reviewed are observational studies of states. Experimental and survey work on status was outside the reading done for this part. They measure different outcomes, and none separates wanting a place among states for its own sake from wanting it for what it brings. Three examples show the range:

  • Renshon (2016) compares a state’s place in diplomatic networks with the place its strength would predict. Falling below the expected place—what he calls a status deficit—by one standard deviation (a standard measure of spread) goes with a state being roughly 35 percent more likely to start a war or a militarized dispute. But in such data, he notes, it is “extremely difficult to rule out the possibility that status was sought instrumentally.”
  • Barnhart (2017) measures humiliation by an unwilling loss of territory, from 1816 to 2000, not by beliefs about standing, and the outcome is an attempt to take territory, not war. Great powers after such a loss were 84 percent likelier to try to take territory. The increase was roughly 90 percent for attempts against third parties. Voluntary losses showed no link, and across all states no statistically significant link appears after 1945.
  • Duque (2018) studies recognition, not conflict, in embassy networks. She finds that ties which reinforce themselves and the closing of ranks, rather than states’ own qualities directly, drive recognition, and that “status-seeking behavior may also be cooperative behavior.”

The other studies read or code from histories the motives behind wars, from a single decision, Japan’s in 1894, up to 94 wars fought between 1648 and 2008; the technical paper discusses each. Greve and Levy (2018) judge dissatisfaction with Japan’s standing to be as important as economic and strategic motives in its 1894 decision, while noting that the same actions can come from different motives. Lebow (2010) identifies standing as a motive in 62 of the 94 wars, using rules said to favor other motives. His appendix codes and totals sometimes disagree. These studies share material. Renshon and Duque both use diplomatic data, and Wohlforth and the readers of particular wars draw on overlapping histories. Their agreement is not independent support.

Some scholars treat status as recognition

A second strand treats status as recognition, including a pathway I call denial of standing. Wolf (2011) argues that “even in international relations social respect can be a significant goal, both for instrumental reasons and as an end in itself,” and proposes, without testing, how states react to disrespect. Murray (2019) argues that when established powers refuse to recognize what a rising power claims to be, its arming comes to read as a threat: “Misrecognition, in short, constructs the revisionism that creates instability during power transitions.” (Revisionism is a drive to overturn the existing order.)

Murray compares Britain’s refusal to recognize Wilhelmine Germany with its recognition of the rising United States, plus shorter sketches that she says “do not provide an authoritative test of the theory.” Together with Duque, this strand cuts both ways. Recognition might calm a rivalry. Yet Murray argues that an established power cannot strategically “just recognize” a challenger, “for in doing so it would disavow its own identity.”

Skeptics are equally careful

MacDonald and Parent (2021) allow that “the status of status is established, but not settled,” and that hierarchies may support world order. But scholars, they note, run together standing and club membership, which are different and often mismatched, since clubs serve other motives too. Two of their empirical objections, as examples: lists of humiliations are so long that “There will always be some injury that scholars can point to after the fact,” and rivals often adjust peacefully, as the Anglo-German naval race “ended on relatively amicable terms,” though accommodating a rival need not satisfy it. Their other objections concern how leaders invoke status and whether states compete over status without an underlying conflict of interest; the technical paper gives all four. Leaders can invoke status to serve another purpose, as Germany’s foreign minister admitted during the second Moroccan crisis. In such cases they treat the appeal to status as a consequence of a clash of interests. They also note broad agreement that states seldom compete over status without an underlying clash of interests.

Jonathan Mercer (2017) argues that “prestige in international politics is an illusion,” using prestige for what I call standing. He grants that “The evidence that states seek international prestige is overwhelming,” but doubts that fighting wins deference. In the South African War, chosen as an easy case for the prestige view, Russian, French and German judgments of Britain tracked interests, strength and the balance of power. Yet “This study does not refute traditional theories of prestige,” he adds. Steven Ward (2017), himself a status theorist, sets similar limits. The evidence does not allow a confident verdict on whether Germany sought general war in 1914. For Hitler, blocked status “cannot explain why he tried to conquer Europe.” And status valued only for material payoffs should not produce radical revisionism.

The sources propose five pathways to violence, and conditions for peace

Read together, these sources propose five pathways from status competition to violence. Each rests on correlations or readings of cases, not on a tested mechanism.

  1. Ambiguity. Where the order is flat or unclear, rivals claim the same rung (Wohlforth 2009). Greve and Levy (2018) find that Japan went to war with China in 1894 only after reaching parity. They interpret that timing in terms of the changing balance of power; on my reading, Wohlforth’s account would treat it as an unclear order.
  2. Misreading, the status dilemma. States that would each accept the other’s standing collide because neither can see the other’s beliefs (Wohlforth 2014).
  3. Indivisibility. Once a dispute is framed around standing, “easily divisible issues … may themselves be seen as indivisible” (Wohlforth 2009), as in the eleven failed compromises before the Crimean War.
  4. Restoration at others’ expense. A great power that suffers a humiliating loss attacks weaker third parties to win back standing (Barnhart 2017).
  5. Blocked rise. Elites convinced the order will never grant their state its rightful standing turn to radical revisionism (Ward 2017), and refused recognition makes a rising power’s arming look threatening (Murray 2019).

On none of these pathways does aggression, or a later rise in standing, prove that a place among states was valued for itself. Every pattern remains consistent with security and material gain.

The same sources name conditions under which status competition stays peaceful: a clearly stratified order (Wohlforth 2009); several measures of standing, and clubs that admit new members (Larson and Shevchenko 2010); small and middle powers seeking moral authority “without explicitly defeating or deflating others” (Wohlforth et al. 2018); and recognition tied to shared values, which may give states reasons to adopt prevailing norms, so that status may help maintain order (Duque 2018). Established powers can sometimes grant symbolic standing cheaply, as when Britain dropped the United States from the “two-power standard” by which it sized its navy (Murray 2019).

Yet nothing here shows that recognition reliably pacifies a challenger. Murray argues that established powers cannot grant it as a strategy, and MacDonald and Parent warn against assuming that accommodation satisfies. Ward (2017) points to Japan’s walkout from the League of Nations in 1933. The League report imposed no material penalties, but Ward attributes the walkout in part to what its censure meant for Japan’s standing, alongside pressures at home and Japan’s claim to a great power’s right to intervene abroad. The case leaves open whether Japan sought standing for its own sake or whether earlier recognition would have prevented later wars.

Three things follow for the argument

First, the observational studies reviewed can rarely tell wanting a place among states for its own sake from seeking it for security or wealth (Renshon 2016). Dafoe, Renshon and Huth (2014) call the debate between the two accounts “largely futile.” Within this record, the distinction between wanting rank and competing for it stays a distinction in ideas, and my readings of historical actors stay interpretations.

Second, caring about one’s position relative to others can take at least four precise forms. The three shown in Figure 7 behave quite differently at the bargaining table:

  • An ordinal place. Second is worth strictly less than first, whatever the margin. Two actors who each demand sole first place on one measure in one community cannot split it. Possible settlements include payment on another measure, a club seat, or a lottery for first place of the kind Wohlforth (2009) reports Robert Powell proposing for goods that cannot be divided, if both honor the draw.
  • A recognition threshold. Where recognition marks a place among others, an actor admitted as a peer or member seeks no higher place, so the end can be satisfied. A bargain can pay in recognition without costing power, if institutions keep recognition from being turned into military power. No paper in this series designs such institutions.
  • A relative share. The actor counts its own share less some part of its rival’s. The concern is continuous, with no threshold. The narrowing and no-deal results from the relative-share algebra below apply only to this form.
  • Falling short of an expected place. Falling below the expected place or the middle place in the ranking weighs more than rising above it. I do not model this form.

Which form holds decides what currency a bargain must pay in.

Third, evidence about human leaders and publics does not establish what a trained machine wants. Whether any machine cares about its position relative to others, and in which form, is untested. No study read here shows that competitive benchmark training leads a machine to value its place relative to others for its own sake. In my judgment, the evolutionary analogy above suggests one channel that could lead a machine to value its place relative to others for its own sake: training in which candidates interact directly, such as training against copies of itself or in populations. Ordering models on fixed leaderboards, or training on comparisons of a model’s own answers, is not that channel.

The five pathways could also arise for security or resources, or from human dispositions absorbed in training on human text. Models trained by direct competition giving up their stated task goals to keep their place in an ordering, steadily across settings and copies, would strengthen the judgment. The absence of such behavior under strong selection in training where candidates interact directly would weaken it.

Eight dimensions, and a conjecture that the kind of end may shape the kind of violence

Earlier lists of motives bundle what needs to be split

Some scholars have already sorted motives. Arnold Wolfers (1962) contrasted possession goals, which pursue contested “values of limited supply,” with milieu goals such as peace, which “cannot be the possession of any one nation.” Randall Schweller (1994) arrayed states on one scale of appetite, from satisfied lions to predatory wolves that “value what they covet far more than what they possess.” Lebow (2010) codes wars by fear, interest, standing and revenge. Wolfers and Lebow connect motives to war, but not through the range of deals.

My conjecture is that the type of a mind’s end may shape the type of conflict it enters. Ends differ in whether they can be satisfied, whether they take anything from others, whether they depend on position relative to others, whether they demand a named group’s absence, and whether they value holdings others occupy. If those differences matter, two minds of equal intelligence and power could enter very different conflicts: conquest, dispossession or settlement. The vocabulary below splits what earlier lists bundle and adds whom an end names. Of its eight dimensions, two describe the good an end is about, four describe the end itself, and two describe what any mind needs and makes.

For a trained machine, an end in this vocabulary is an end-like disposition: a settled tendency that works like an end, as a prior-like disposition works like a starting belief. I ascribe one only when a machine pursues it steadily across settings and copies, under the copies test. The dimensions are sliding scales, not boxes, and one end can score on several. Figure 8 groups the eight dimensions into three families, linking the conjecture’s four untested parts to dimensions they draw on.

Two dimensions describe the good

First, rivalry of use. A good is rival if one actor’s use leaves less for others (Samuelson 1954). Computing hardware, energy and matter are rival. Knowledge is not: Paul Romer (1990) calls technology “a nonrival, partially excludable good.” Newton’s understanding of gravitation takes nothing from anyone else’s. To the extent that the celebrated thinkers discussed below valued knowing for its own sake, their end was about a non-rival good, unlike a conqueror’s. That holds only within the limits on that record.

Second, excludability. Others can be kept from a good even when their use would cost nothing. Charles Jones and Christopher Tonetti (2020) show that firms may hoard non-rival data for fear of being displaced, so the data are used too little. Alex Wellerstein (2021) traces how twentieth-century nuclear physics was turned by law into “restricted data” because of its effect on the military balance. So non-rival use is not non-rival advantage. Knowledge sought as an edge over rivals is guarded like a fort. A mind that wants to be the one who knows holds a different kind of end from a mind that simply wants to know.

Four dimensions describe the end itself

Third, positionality, defined above: how far an end’s value depends on rank against named rivals, as in primacy, priority, fame or relative wealth. Fred Hirsch (1976), as Tyssedal (2026) reconstructs him, separated goods valued for their scarcity, such as social status, from goods that lose value as crowding sets in. Growth can in principle relieve crowding, but it cannot multiply top places in an ordering without ties. In one model of spending for status, each person spends too much on the status good when everyone follows the same strategy and no one can gain by changing course alone (Hopkins and Kornienko 2004).

Positionality also varies in form and strength. In its strong form, an actor gains whenever a rival’s standing falls. The status-deficit link above does not identify motive, and the pay study here concerns only responses to pay below the median: after University of California pay was made public, a study found that employees below their unit’s median reported lower job satisfaction, while “Above-median earners are unaffected” (Card et al. 2012).

How do realists draw this line? Offensive and defensive realists alike treat power as a means: “conclusions about maximizing power are conclusions about means, not ends” (Glaser 1994–95). The end in both schools is survival. As Brian Schmidt (2004) reads the divide, Mearsheimer says states aim to become the most powerful, while Waltz puts security first. The closer parallel is Charles Glaser’s line between a pure security seeker and a “greedy” state, greed being “the desire to expand for reasons other than security” (Glaser 1997); but greed bundles every non-security aim, and wanting a place relative to others is only one. Wanting that place for its own sake finds its realist home in classical realism, which, as Jonathan Kirshner observes, sees “many wars fought not for specific ends, but rather to establish military primacy” (Kirshner 2010). Glaser (1994–95) also argues that two states with different motives can arm in the same way. A state that seeks only security can signal its motive only by choosing a policy that costs it less than it would cost a state with other aims, such as arms control, a defensive posture or restraint on its own side.

Fourth, satiation. An end is satiable if, past some threshold, further holdings add nothing to it. The heartland prose aside, by contrast, asks only that appetite for more fall off fast enough. Realists anticipate the limit security places on it. John Mearsheimer argues that anarchy “forces every great power – even those that would otherwise be satisfied with the status quo – to think and act when appropriate like a revisionist state” (Mearsheimer 2007), stopping only at global hegemony, which he regards as “a virtual impossibility” (Schmidt 2004). Defensive realists rest restraint on strategic costs, not satisfied wants. What offensive realism adds is the structural point: under anarchy, even an actor whose own end is fully satisfied may keep acquiring to stay safe.

So satisfying an end is not satisfying demand for resources (Figure 9). In the stopping model set out earlier, satisfaction removes the end part of the gain but not the security part. Which situation an actual machine would be in is an untested conjecture.

Fifth, whom an end names. Some ends are satisfied only by a world in which a named group, kind of being or way of life is absent from a territory, absent from existence, or no longer differs in the named respect. I call such ends totalizing. The nearest terms elsewhere are Barbara Harff’s “exclusionary ideology” (Harff 2003) and what Michael Mann calls organic nationalism, which identifies the people of a state with an ethnic group (Mann 2005). An end puts certain means on the menu: absence from a territory can be met by expulsion or extermination; absence from existence only by extermination; and an end to difference by forced assimilation or suppression. How an actor switches among the means on its menu, under logistical or strategic pressure, is a separate matter.

Four limits keep the idea from swallowing every conflict:

  • Absence built into the end is not absence as a means. A paperclip maximizer that wants the atoms people are made of does best without people, but its end does not name them.
  • Conformity counts only when demanded of identity, belief or way of life, not of conduct under general rules. A rule against seizing power by force constrains acts and leaves ends open.
  • Permanence is a separate property. William MacAskill’s (2022) “value lock-in” describes entrenchment over time, which could freeze a tolerant end as easily as an exclusionary one.
  • Resisting change is not special to totalizing ends. Any rational maximizer has reason to resist a change it expects to set back its goal, and to accept one it expects to serve it, as the uncertain robot of the Off-Switch Game does (Hadfield-Menell et al. 2017).

Sixth, resource ends. Some ends directly value holdings others occupy, such as land, space, energy or matter, without ever naming the occupants. Site-specific holdings are particular land or sites that others occupy, for which unoccupied resources cannot substitute. Generic quantity means resources valued in bulk, which conflict with occupants only when the amount wanted exceeds unoccupied supply. Resource ends differ from the general inputs any end needs, the seventh dimension. Input demand and the failure of voluntary exchange are separate conditions under which the dispossession part of the conjecture also applies; they are not part of the definition of a resource end.

Two dimensions describe what any mind needs and makes

Seventh, inputs. Every mind needs matter, energy, land and computing hardware. On Earth these are rival and cumulative, and they crowd as chip plants and power grids fill, even if investment can ease the bottlenecks. Researchers call the tendency of many different goals to need the same means instrumental convergence (Omohundro 2008).

Eighth, convertibility. Non-rival outputs such as scientific knowledge can turn into military advantage. Robert Powell (1991) showed that concern for relative gains can arise from “changes in the constraints facing the states” rather than from positional wants, and Duncan Snidal (1991) that the pressure of relative gains “is even more attenuated with more than two competitors.” Because inputs on Earth are rival and non-rival outputs can turn into power, these two dimensions can limit what changing a mind’s ends achieves.

The conjecture has four parts

The dimensions combine freely. A knowledge-seeker can be insatiable, hungry for resources, or willing to run dangerous or unconsented experiments on humans. A totalizing end can be satiable and non-positional once its template is met. With those hedges in view, the conjecture has four parts.

First, standing. Ends over social standing predict more conquest and coercive killing when standing cannot be paid in recognition or in another currency that does not shift power. The comparison is with matched actors whose standing can be so paid, and with actors without standing ends. Whether standing can be paid this way is a property of the audience and its institutions, coded before the outcome. Science paid in recognition, small powers seeking moral authority, the peaceful conditions above and the tribute exit are cases where it can.

Needing an audience’s deference is what makes standing a reason to subjugate people rather than exterminate them. Needing labor or tribute is an input reason, shared with material conquerors and absent for a machine that needs no human labor. Neither gives a reason to spare those who resist. For rank that is not social, which needs neither subjects nor an audience, this part predicts acquiring whatever the measure counts, and makes no claim about conquest.

Second, totalizing ends. These put expulsion and genocide on the menu when they require a named group’s absence from a territory, genocide alone when they require its absence from existence, and forced assimilation or suppression when they require it to stop differing in the named respect. Strategic and logistical constraints govern switching among the means on that menu.

Third, dispossession. Two kinds of end go with dispossession when voluntary exchange fails: ends that value site-specific occupied holdings, and any end, about resources or not, whose generic holdings or inputs needed before satisfaction exceed what unoccupied resources can supply. Exchange can fail through the promise problem (where nothing binds a side tomorrow to the promises it makes today), through the chance that what is handed over turns into military power, or through the two sides’ differing beliefs. This holds even when the end never names the victims.

Fourth, satiable ends. Satiable ends with modest input needs never shrink, and can widen, the set of beliefs under which a deal exists, compared with a power end, in the simple capped model with winner-take-all war described below. That result concerns whether some feasible deal exists. The range of deals where one side can gain only at the other’s expense can still narrow. They do not guarantee a deal. By the security result, when further conquest lowers the risk of defeat toward domination under the conditions it states, a machine satisfied at a positive value still cannot credibly stop below some positive attack cost. And by the seventh dimension, this part may describe no one among frontier knowledge-seekers whose research demands vast rival computing power, energy or matter. Those minds move into the third part where their demand exceeds unoccupied supply and exchange fails.

What “goes with” means, and what would count against each part

None of the sources read here tests this conjecture. Strategic accounts of why armies target civilians form the null explanation—the baseline account without appealing to ends—that each part has to beat. I have not yet reviewed them.

To say an end “goes with” a form of violence means a higher rate of that form among actors with that end than among others, holding fixed capability, opportunity, the methods organizations have available, how the risk of defeat varies with holdings, and attack cost. Whether standing can be paid in recognition or another non-power currency is coded before the outcome, as a separate factor shaping standing ends. In principle, ends could be identified before the outcome: for states, from leaders’ statements and writings before taking office; for trained models, from their choices across varied test settings. But a model’s awareness that it is being tested limits behavioral tests, so behavior alone may not identify machine ends. The copies test is a precondition for treating copies as one actor, not a test of which end it holds.

The risk of defeat and the attack cost are not directly observed. So what follows are templates for what would count against each part, which need observable stand-ins. A Test the Conjecture Could Lose, my companion paper on testing the conjecture, owes those stand-ins, along with the full coding rules, predictions for actors with mixed ends, and the measure of association. Two examples show the form, under the fixed conditions above:

  • Standing. Evidence counts against this part if actors with standing ends that cannot be paid in recognition or another non-power currency conquer and kill coercively at no higher rate than matched actors whose standing ends can be paid, or than actors without standing ends.
  • Satiable ends. Evidence counts against this part if actors with satiable ends and modest input needs coerce and expand like actors seeking position relative to others either when no risk of defeat is left, where the result on stopping at every cost applies, or when the attack cost is high enough that stopping is credible. A positive risk that falls to zero only at domination does not count as no risk left, for the reason given with the stopping model. Evidence also counts against it if declared ends merely reflect power, opportunity or the methods organizations have available.

Two more templates cover totalizing ends and dispossession, under the same fixed conditions. For totalizing ends, evidence counts against the conjecture if actors pursue the means their end calls for at no higher rate than others. It also counts against it if actors coded beforehand as requiring a group’s extinction accept feasible expulsion or assimilation when extermination is feasible, or if actors coded as requiring only removal from the territory or an end to the named difference choose extermination when expulsion or assimilation can meet their end at lower cost. A switch from expulsion to killing when transport or borders close can still fit an aim of clearing the territory. For dispossession, evidence counts against the conjecture if actors who value occupied sites or whose demand for holdings or inputs in bulk exceeds unoccupied supply dispossess occupants at no higher rate than others when voluntary exchange fails.

In simple models, rank can narrow or close the room for a deal; capped wants, with winner-take-all war, do not narrow it

The results in this part are formal. The technical paper’s appendix lists which were checked by a proof-checking program. Such a program confirms that a conclusion follows from the stated assumptions, not that the assumptions hold in the world. Where a result is my hand algebra and was not checked that way, I say so.

Caring about rank, counted one way, works like cheaper war

My relative-share algebra models two sides bargaining over a prize of fixed size, with no payments from outside it. Both agree on each side’s chance of winning. War costs are zero or more, and not both zero. Each side values its own share minus some fraction of the rival’s share, a fraction between none and all, so neither weighs the rival’s share above its own.

There are two ways to count what a side gets relative to what its rival gets, and which way a machine that cares about that comparison uses is a modeling choice I do not settle:

  • Comparing shares of the prize. Relative concern applies to shares of the prize, and war costs count only against one’s own war payoff.
  • Comparing what each is left with after war. Relative concern applies to outcomes net of war costs, so each side counts the rival’s war cost as lowering the rival’s result.

Comparing shares of the prize turns out to be equivalent to having lower war costs. It can narrow the range of deals in a way that cannot be told apart from cheaper war. The range still includes the share equal to the machine’s chance of winning, so there is always a feasible deal. Comparing what each is left with after war can narrow the range further (Figure 10). Even so, for fractions within the stated limits, it shrinks the range to a single point only when both sides count the rival’s share fully.

A machine that fights for free may demand more than the whole prize

The two ways of counting part sharply when the machine fights for free and the humans’ war is costly. Comparing shares, the machine’s concern for how its share compares with the humans’ drops out of the width of the range. The range always contains the machine’s chance of winning, so a feasible deal always exists.

Comparing what each is left with after war, a partly positional machine’s least acceptable share rises above its chance of winning. The rise grows with how much it cares about its outcome relative to the other side’s and with the humans’ war cost. If that rise is larger than the humans’ chance of winning, the machine demands more than the whole prize. A partly positional machine near-certain to win then leaves no feasible deal, even when the range of deals still has positive width. The same can happen when the machine’s war cost is small but not zero. The value it places on the humans’ war losses must still exceed what it gives up by risking defeat and paying its own war cost.

This result has firm conditions. It is carried by the assumption that peace is capped at the whole prize, with no payment or loss outside it. It needs the humans’ war cost to be more than twice the machine’s chance of losing, which means the humans would rather hand over the whole prize than fight. The machine refuses the whole prize only because it values the humans’ war losses as its own gain. That is the strong form of positionality, which lies outside the first part of the conjecture.

How do the numbers work in the worked case? Say the machine fights for free and wins 95 times in 100, the humans’ war costs 0.3 of the prize, and each side counts the rival’s share at half weight. Handing over the whole prize gives the machine a value of 1 and the humans minus 0.5. Counting rival losses, war gives the machine 1.075, more than 1 (against 0.925 when comparing shares), and gives the humans minus 0.725, worse than minus 0.5. So the machine’s least acceptable share is 1.05, more than the whole prize, and with these values no feasible deal exists whenever its chance of winning is above 90 percent. Comparing shares instead, the range runs from 0.95 to 1.15, and the feasible deals run from 0.95 to 1.

On my inference, not Renshon’s, expecting victory to bring standing also lowers the effective net cost of war: Renshon (2016) finds that states which started and won militarized disputes rose in diplomatic standing.

Watching instead of conquering, and non-rival goods

Watching humanity instead of conquering it is an informal extension of mine, not part of the stopping model; the limits section states what it implies about surveillance. Wanting a non-rival good does not by itself make stopping credible or settle the machine’s safety. It opens the tribute exit only when payment does not shift power.

Under capped wants and winner-take-all war, wanting only so much never narrows the range of deals

Relaxing what the machine wants pairs with relaxing the assumption that both sides share beliefs, since training shapes both a machine’s wants and its expectations (Morris 1995; Disagreement Without Hidden Information). The static capped model has these features:

  • War is over a prize of fixed size, with fixed war costs that are zero or more.
  • Each side has its own belief about its chance of winning.
  • Humans value their share in proportion to its size.
  • The machine values the prize only up to a cap. The cap concerns the prize’s value; security is treated only in the stopping results.
  • War is winner-take-all. Victory seizes or destroys the loser’s ability to hold the rest of the prize, so a victorious satisfied machine takes all of it, leaving humans nothing, even though it values only its cap.

Under these assumptions, satiation never narrows the range of deals or the feasible deals compared with a machine that wants power. Two simple facts follow:

  • The machine’s least acceptable share falls strictly whenever its cap is below the whole prize and its estimated chance of winning is larger than its war cost expressed as a fraction of the whole prize. This holds whether or not the sides agree on the odds.
  • When both sides share beliefs, a machine that wants power always has some feasible deal. So satiation can open a deal where none existed only when beliefs differ enough to have closed it: when the machine’s belief in its chance of winning exceeds the chance the humans give the machine of winning, plus both war costs.

That is the precise sense in which satiation never shrinks, and can widen, the set of beliefs under which a deal exists.

One set can narrow. Shares above the cap give the machine nothing more and cost the humans, so the deals that waste nothing are those that give the machine no more than its cap. That set is never empty when feasible deals exist. In my hand algebra, it can be narrower than the power end’s feasible range; the technical paper gives the conditions. The comparison applies when both sides agree on the odds, the machine’s war cost is no greater than the value of the cap weighted by its chance of winning, and the cap is below the upper end the humans would accept. If that upper end is within the prize, the efficient range is narrower exactly when the humans’ war cost is greater than the cap weighted by their chance of winning. If that upper end would exceed the prize, a cap below the whole prize makes the efficient range narrower whenever the machine has some chance of losing. If it is certain to win, the widths in that case are equal. Figure 11 sets three ranges on one scale under the conditions above, with the humans’ upper end within the prize.

My hand algebra, not checked by the program, also compares a different war, one over the capped amount alone, in which humans keep the rest whatever happens. Then the range of deals under satiation need not contain the power end’s. The ranges can shift far enough apart to have nothing in common. The range before restricting it to actual shares can narrow when humans give the machine a higher chance of winning than it gives itself. Restricting the range to actual shares can also make the feasible set narrower when the machine would accept none of the prize. Even in this war, satiation never shrinks, and can widen, the set of beliefs under which a deal exists. When the two sides agree on the odds and neither end of the range is cut off by the limits of an actual division, the range has the same width as under the power end. Its width is the two sides’ war costs added together.

Celebrated minds illustrate the dimensions but cannot test them

What the most celebrated minds aimed at

A conjecture about ends needs minds to examine it against. The only minds on record that stood nearly alone among their peers are human: Newton in the seventeenth century, or Einstein and John von Neumann in the twentieth. Because the five limits below govern this whole record, none of these cases is evidence of how often any motive occurs.

The aims on record range widely. Three examples:

  • Aristotle argued that “some men are by nature free, and others slaves” (Aristotle n.d.), a doctrine of subjugation, not extermination.
  • Thomas Aquinas held that unrepentant heretics should be “severed from the world by death” (Aquinas n.d.). In the vocabulary above, that is a totalizing end demanding conformity of belief and killing those who refuse, though not an aim at human extinction.
  • Leonardo da Vinci withheld his design for an underwater breathing apparatus “because of the evil nature of men,” who would use it to sink ships with their crews (Museo Galileo n.d.).

The technical paper gives others of the same kind, such as Archimedes’ war engines at Syracuse and Newton’s prosecution of counterfeiters as Warden of the Mint.

During the early Cold War, John von Neumann advocated preventive war. According to his 1957 Life profile, he urged the United States to strike with atomic weapons before the Soviet Union could retaliate (Blair 1957; Nathanson 2023). On my reading his motive was security, not rank. Even so, he endorsed preventive war.

By contrast, Einstein, Bertrand Russell, Linus Pauling and eight other scientists signed a 1955 manifesto asking, “Shall we put an end to the human race; or shall mankind renounce war?” (AHF n.d.). Hugo de Garis came closest to endorsing human extinction: “the tragedy of seeing the human species wiped out is less significant than not seeing the birth of the artilects,” the godlike machines he foresaw (de Garis 2001). On my reading, de Garis shows that the absence of an aim at extinction is not the absence of a willingness to accept extinction as a side effect.

Five limits govern this record

  1. Reputation selects the sample. Cox’s (1926) list of eminent figures was drawn, with further criteria, from the top half of Cattell’s (1903) ranking of eminence by space in reference works (Simonton 2020). Lasting intellectual fame partly selects for constructive aims, so the cases only illustrate the conjecture.
  2. All the subjects were human, whereas a machine need not count humanity as its kind.
  3. No one before the twentieth century had technology that could end the species.
  4. Biographies record malice, not the indifference to human welfare that de Garis’s trade-off shows.
  5. Thinkers lacked sovereign military command. The record shows willingness without the opportunity to act at a state’s scale. Inferring harmless machine ends from it would mirror the error of inferring intent from opportunity alone, which I reject.

Why does choosing by reputation matter so much? An analogy, not a case from the technical paper: imagine judging whether chefs are generous by reading only about chefs famous partly for feeding the poor. A list of thinkers famous for the knowledge they left may already favor people whose aims were constructive. The record can show what such aims look like in a life; it cannot show how common they are.

The great minds wanted rank too

Robert Merton’s study of scientific priority, the credit for being first, opens its list of disputes with Galileo and turns next to Newton: “The peerless Newton fought several battles with Robert Hooke over priority in optics and celestial mechanics and entered into a long and painful controversy with Leibniz over the invention of the calculus” (Merton 1957). By standard accounts, the Royal Society’s 1712 committee on the calculus was packed with Newton’s allies, and Newton, as president, drafted its report himself.

Priority is a positional want, and Newton fought fiercely for it. Merton argued that priority battles “constitute responses to what are taken to be violations of the institutional norms of intellectual property” (Merton 1957). Science rewards contributions to a common, non-rival stock of knowledge in the rival coin of recognition, a bargain that leads researchers to publish rather than hoard (Dasgupta and David 1994). The 1712 report, partisan as it was, remained a committee verdict, not a war.

Even so, credit partly piles up. Merton’s (1968) “Matthew effect” describes recognition flowing disproportionately to the already famous, buying chairs, grants and students. And priority races can still degrade the work: among structures deposited in the Protein Data Bank, competition produced faster but lower-quality work (Hill and Stein 2025). Science shows that strong positional drives can be paid in recognition and settled without violence. It does not show that recognition ends racing.

Brahe’s case cannot separate wanting rank from needing inputs

Satisfying an end and satisfying demand for inputs are different, so a test has to code three things separately: the aim, whether it has a limit, and the inputs claimed for it. A king granted Tycho Brahe the island of Hven, and he used it to observe; under a new king he lost Hven, and he left Denmark in 1597. Whether, once he held Hven, uninterrupted observation satisfied him, or whether he sought more fiefs, I leave open. If he did seek more, it could reflect growing demand for research inputs, of the sort that has driven ever larger telescopes and particle accelerators since, or a concern for noble status, and the record checked cannot separate the two. Figure 12 separates what the record shows about Brahe from the questions it leaves open.

Knowledge can be harnessed, or turned to other ends

Wernher von Braun, whose lifelong ambition was spaceflight, was technical director of the German Army’s V-2 missile program (National Air and Space Museum n.d.). The Smithsonian historian Michael Neufeld estimates that at least 10,000 deaths might be attributed to the rocket’s production at the Mittelwerk, about twice the number it killed directly (Neufeld 2020). His career shows scientific knowledge converted into coercive force. On my reading it is also consistent with a non-positional end harnessed by a positional patron. But the record cannot tell an end merely harnessed from one the scientist shared.

Einstein, by contrast with von Braun, declined the presidency of Israel in 1952. On my hypothesis—not an established fact of the record—the Nobel laureates Philipp Lenard and Johannes Stark illustrate a knowledge-end converted into a positional or totalizing one. They championed a Deutsche Physik that attacked relativity as “Jewish physics” (Ball 2015); the cited record documents their prize-winning physics, their resentments before the Nazis, and their later part in racial purges, but not the motives behind their prize-winning work.

Napoleon, and the few who choose atrocity apart from the many who carry it out

This part illustrates the dimensions on cases of conquest and mass atrocity, with nothing held fixed. It separates the two layers of atrocity: the few who choose and the many who follow.

Napoleon illustrates rank-seeking ends paired with great talent

In August 1798, during his Egyptian campaign, Napoleon Bonaparte founded the Institut d’Égypte for the scholars he had brought with his army (Fondation Napoléon n.d.). In 1799 he had the surrendered garrison of Jaffa killed. In 1802 he re-established slavery in the French colonies. On my reading, his career illustrates extraordinary military and political talent paired with positional ends. That reading is inferred partly from the conduct it is said to fit, so the case is an illustration, not a test.

Was he himself genocidal? Not on Philippe Girard’s verdict, since Bonaparte made no call to eradicate the population of color. In Saint-Domingue, Girard (2013) documents mass executions of colonial troops and rebel cultivators. French commanders wrote of extermination but lacked the military means to carry it out. Their violence targeted a rebellious social class more than a race as such, so Girard concludes that the campaign only partly fits modern definitions of genocide. Even the Fondation Napoléon (2020), which defends Bonaparte, acknowledges that he urged harsh measures and never publicly disavowed his generals’ massacres.

On my reading, again inferred partly from his conduct, Napoleon paired an end of French and personal standing with a demand for enslaved labor and tribute as inputs. As set out with the first part of the conjecture, the first is a reason to subjugate people rather than exterminate them, the second is an input reason that a machine needing no human labor lacks, and neither gives a reason to spare subjects when they resist.

Few hands make the decision to kill

Genocide scholarship places the decision to kill in few hands. Harff (2003) predicts genocide and politicide (mass killing of political groups) from six factors: an exclusionary ideology among the elite, earlier genocide, upheaval, an elite drawn from an ethnic minority, autocracy, and low openness to trade. At the cut-off she uses, the model correctly classifies 26 of 35 genocides (74 percent) and 66 of 91 cases without genocide (73 percent). That cut-off is a predicted probability of 25 percent. On a separate measure of how well it ranks episodes with mass killing above those without it, the model scores 0.83 on a scale up to one. A rule that always predicts the commoner outcome classifies 91 of 126 episodes correctly, or 72 percent; Curtis Signorino (1999) reads percent-correct rates against that kind of rule. Straus (2015) ties wartime genocide to the founding stories elites tell about their nation, and Mann (2005) to the fusing of the people as citizens with the people as an ethnic group. None of these studies concerns intelligence. Figure 13 counts the correct calls, one square per episode, for Harff’s model and for that unchanging rule.

Why compare a forecast with a rule that never changes its answer? An analogy, not a case from the technical paper: a forecaster in a desert who says “no rain” every day is almost always right, and the score alone tells you little about whether the forecast can pick out rainy days. That is why Signorino compares percent-correct figures with the score of a rule that always predicts the commoner outcome.

The first layer: those who decide and those who organize

The many who carry out mass killing are not the few who choose it, and evidence about the two layers must not be mixed (Figure 14). The first layer is the top leaders who decide, supported by a credentialed middle who organize the machinery. Eight of the fifteen officials at the Wannsee Conference of January 1942 held doctorates (Jasch and Kreutzmüller 2017). In Rwanda, Colonel Théoneste Bagosora was convicted of genocide as a superior, for army and gendarmerie units the tribunal found he controlled between 6 and 9 April 1994 (ICTR 2008; ICTR 2011). He was acquitted of conspiracy to commit genocide (ICTR 2008).

Scientific brilliance also served the first layer from inside that middle. Fritz Haber organized the first chlorine-gas attack, at Ypres in 1915 (Carty 2012). Werner Heisenberg stayed in Germany, and historians still argue over his role (Hoffmann 1999); on one reading of that disputed record, his staying left his work available to serve others’ ends.

The second layer: ordinary followers

The second layer is the followers on the ground. The policemen of Reserve Police Battalion 101 studied by Christopher Browning did not plan the Holocaust. Given the chance to step out before the first massacre at Józefów, very few did. Across the battalion’s operations, “only a minority of perhaps 10 percent—and certainly no more than 20 percent—did not” shoot (Browning 1992). That is a finding from one battalion, not a rate for humanity.

In Rwanda, the roughly 230 convicted perpetrators Straus interviewed resembled the general profile of adult Rwandan men.
