They were driven by wartime fear, pressure from peers, and killing framed as civic duty: “Once the government told people it was their duty to go out and attack neighbors, it happened very quickly” (Straus 2006). Reanalyses of Stanley Milgram’s shock experiments likewise qualify simple accounts of blind obedience. Of the experimenter’s prods, “the one most resembling an order was least successful” (Haslam, Reicher and Birney 2014), and compliance rose when the experimenter appealed to the study’s scientific value. Stephen Reicher and colleagues call this identification-based followership (Reicher, Haslam and Smith 2012), and it works alongside conformity, peer pressure and fear.

The pairings map loosely onto the record

I read the historical cases as loose illustrations of how the conjecture pairs ends with forms of political violence.

  • Coercive massacres such as Jaffa can illustrate positional ends, where killing punishes defiance and compels submission. But other readings of Jaffa, logistical or about broken promises by released prisoners not to fight again, also exist; the historical citation is owed. Napoleon’s ends are read partly from the conduct they are said to fit.
  • Extermination, expulsion or forced assimilation based on identity, where the end names the target group, illustrates totalizing ends.
  • Taking land illustrates the dispossession part. This part applies when voluntary exchange fails and either the actor values a particular occupied site or the holdings or inputs it wants in bulk exceed unoccupied supply. The goal is the land, and native peoples are removed or destroyed because they stand on it. That theme is reflected in the title of Patrick Wolfe’s 2006 article, “Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native,” cited for its title only.

In practice the pairings overlap, and the worst twentieth-century regimes plausibly fused positional and totalizing ends.

Genocide is not extinction

The two-layer account offers a possible analogy, not an empirical finding, for atrocity and domination carried out with AI under human direction. There a machine acts as an obedient second layer, or a resourceful credentialed middle, for a small human elite. The analogy establishes nothing about a machine that does the choosing itself. A machine’s end could name humanity itself, a possibility the human record cannot test. Nor does that record offer any comfort about a machine whose resource ends simply require the matter and energy humanity occupies. Nothing in the human record establishes what a machine wants.

What is not modelled, what is unmeasured or unread, and what would change the answer

Four things are not modelled

  • The stopping model from Satiation Is Not Enough describes a machine stopping on its own against a risk of defeat set from outside, with no bargain between the sides.
  • The relative-share algebra leaves out payments from outside the prize. It covers only the continuous relative-share form of caring about one’s position relative to others, not ordinal places, recognition thresholds, or falling short of an expected place.
  • No paper in this series designs institutions that pay in recognition while keeping recognition from turning into military power.
  • The four parts of the conjecture treat ends as fixed before the outcome, whereas actors’ ends may shift during a conflict.

Much is unmeasured or unread

  • The conjecture is untested.
  • The exploratory screenings of biographies in the technical paper’s appendix used one AI coder, with no second rater, and they are subject to the selection and opportunity limits of the record set out above.
  • Whether Brahe sought further fiefs is open.
  • Powell’s (1991) formal model was not checked.
  • Valentino’s (2004) typology of mass killing is known only at second hand. I leave it out of the analysis. Wolfe (2006), Harff’s 2003 table, Valentino’s wider table and part of Straus (2015) are unread. Straus (2006) and Browning (1992) are quoted from a publisher’s release and a published excerpt.
  • Strategic accounts of civilian targeting, the null explanation each part of the conjecture has to beat, have not been reviewed; those reads are owed. So I cannot yet say what ends predict about the form of violence beyond strategic incentives.

The results themselves narrow the role left to ends

Taken together, my own results narrow what ends alone can do once input demand and security are counted:

  • Input demand. A non-rival knowledge-seeker can move into the dispossession part of the conjecture when its demand for rival inputs exceeds unoccupied supply and exchange fails.
  • Security. Under the security result, continued expansion can remain the better choice below a positive attack cost even after the machine’s end is satisfied at a positive value. From that point onward, the risk of defeat must never rise as holdings grow, be lower at domination than at any earlier holding, and make defeat certain nowhere below domination.
  • Beliefs. In the static capped model, satiation opens a deal where none existed only when beliefs differ.

Once these are counted, the kinds of end that still change predicted conduct in this framework are few:

  • positional ends, under the first part of the conjecture and under the after-war way of counting;
  • totalizing ends, under the second part;
  • ends valuing site-specific occupied holdings, under the third part; and
  • satiation, but only where conquest does not lower the risk of defeat or where beliefs differ, under the fourth part.

For a machine that fights cheaply and needs large rival inputs, the difference in behavior due to ends alone may therefore be small.

What I do not claim

I make no claim about what any machine wants, whether recognition reliably pacifies, any historical base rate, or whether intelligence brings any particular end with it.

What would change the answer

Several of my judgments are provisional:

  • keeping rationality as a starting assumption while relaxing wants first, and contrasting machine ends with state preferences;
  • when knowing outweighs concern for position relative to others, and the analogy between evolution and training in which candidates interact directly;
  • the informal extension about a satisfied machine watching humanity; and
  • the illustrative readings of von Neumann, Napoleon, Heisenberg, and Lenard and Stark.

These judgments would shift in three cases:

  • if a changed game, or the rules of thumb of limited minds, explained the misfit in Bennett and Stam (2004);
  • according to whether models trained by direct competition give up task goals for the sake of their place among other models across settings and copies; or
  • if ends coded independently fail to predict the kind of violence and whether actors stop acquiring resources, with capability, opportunity, the methods organizations have available, how the risk of defeat varies with holdings, and attack cost held fixed.

Watching instead of conquering means watching very closely

There is a sobering implication about surveillance. When the risk of defeat is zero at domination, the sufficient condition above for stopping at every cost holds only if no risk is left from the stopping point up. If watching were to replace conquest and remove the risk that humanity builds a rival, it would have to involve surveillance and control intrusive enough to stop any community from building one. Imperfect watching that leaves some risk leaves the security result’s pressure to expand in force when its other conditions hold. Lowering the risk can still make stopping more valuable to the machine, when that gain outweighs the cost of watching. Some way of verifying humanity’s restraint without surveillance could take watching’s place.

What to take away

There are four things to take away.

  • A vocabulary. It separates the group one is ranked against from the audience that confers rank, holding a rank from wanting one, and wanting rank from competing for it. It also keeps status, standing, recognition, prestige and respect apart.
  • What the studies show. The observational studies of states reviewed establish associations and readings of cases, not tested mechanisms. Their five pathways to violence remain consistent with security and material motives.
  • An untested conjecture. Eight dimensions state a conjecture that the kind of end may shape the kind of violence. Its link from ends to violence is illustrated by the record, not derived. Each part has to beat the strategic account of civilian targeting, which is not yet reviewed. Its tests await the measures and coding rules owed in A Test the Conjecture Could Lose.
  • Formal results in one kind of war. Comparing shares of the prize, caring about what one gets relative to what the other side gets works like cheaper war: it can narrow the range of deals without emptying it. Counting the rival’s war losses as a gain, with peace capped at the whole prize, can leave no feasible deal. In the capped model with winner-take-all war, wanting only so much never narrows the range of deals, lowers the machine’s least acceptable share whenever its cap is below the whole prize and its belief in winning exceeds its war cost, and opens a deal where none existed only when beliefs differ, though the set of deals that waste nothing can narrow. And in the stopping model from Satiation Is Not Enough, security keeps a satisfied machine expanding below a positive attack cost when conquest lowers its risk of defeat, under the conditions of the security result.

Where to read more

  • Ends, Rank and Conflict: A Vocabulary of Ends and a Conjecture about Conflict, the technical paper, gives the formal conditions, the algebra and the list of historical cases in its appendix.
  • The War Baseline supplies the four starting assumptions, the range of deals, the promise problem at a machine’s arrival, and the forts model with its tribute and heartland exits.
  • Disagreement Without Hidden Information supplies the idea that training shapes a machine’s expectations, so the two sides can disagree without hidden information.
  • When Is a Machine an Actor? supplies the test for when copies of a model count as one actor.
  • Satiation Is Not Enough supplies the stopping model and the six results on when a satisfied machine can credibly stop.
  • A Test the Conjecture Could Lose is where the observable measures, coding rules, mixed-end predictions and measure of association for testing the conjecture are owed.
